meta.blurb: At a crowded sale, old Father Abraham answers a worried crowd with the sayings of Poor Richard: work hard, spend wisely and never run into debt. Benjamin Franklin's famous speech is funny, sharp and surprisingly modern.
meta.bible: Benjamin Franklin: American printer, writer and scientist, born in Boston in 1706, who worked in Philadelphia. Poor Richard's Almanack: the yearly book that Franklin published for about twenty-five years, ending with the edition for 1758. Poor Richard and Richard Saunders: the invented author of the almanack. Father Abraham: the plain, white-haired old man in the tale who speaks to the crowd. The Way to Wealth: the speech, first printed in the 1758 almanack and later published on its own. Vendue: a public sale of goods, where people bid. Heaven: the power the old man says we must also depend on. Job: a man in the Bible who suffered and was later prosperous. Lent: the forty days of fasting before Easter. Easter: the Christian spring festival. Spain: the country named in the speech. Indies: the lands from which Spain received gold. Reason: the old man's word for good sense. Many of the sayings are older proverbs that Franklin reworded. Voice and tone: lively, witty, practical and kind; the old sayings are paraphrased in plain modern English; no invented numbers or quotes.

beats.scene: A farmer reads a small book by candlelight at a kitchen table
beats.summary: An almanack held a calendar, the weather and short sayings, and Poor Richard's sayings were about work and money.

beats.summary: In 1758 Franklin gathered the best sayings into one speech, which became The Way to Wealth.

beats.scene: A crowd waits outside a shop for a sale of goods to begin
beats.summary: Richard says he stopped at a sale of goods where a crowd was waiting and talking about hard times.

beats.summary: A man asks old Father Abraham whether the heavy taxes will ruin the country.

beats.summary: Father Abraham stands, promises short advice, and begins by quoting Poor Richard.

beats.summary: Diligence is the mother of good luck, and God gives all things to industry.

beats.summary: It is easier to build two chimneys than to keep one in fuel: gain is uncertain, but expense is constant.

beats.summary: Get what you can, and what you get hold; it is the stone that will turn all your lead into gold.

beats.summary: Industry and frugality are not enough: be humble, and remember that success also depends on Heaven's blessing.

beats.scene: Richard Saunders sits on his horse at the edge of the crowd, surprised
beats.summary: Richard realises the old man has studied all his almanacks for twenty-five years.

beats.scene: A man holds up cloth for a new coat, then puts it down
beats.summary: Richard resolves to be better for the echo of it: he meant to buy cloth for a new coat, but will wear his old one a little longer.

beats.scene: A worn old coat hangs by a window beside a neat stack of coins
beats.summary: Ending: work hard, spend wisely, avoid debt; the speech has been read in many countries.

B1B2: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston in 1706 and later worked as a printer in Philadelphia. Every year he published a small book called Poor Richard's Almanack.
An almanack was a yearly book with a calendar and guesses about the weather. Poor Richard also filled it with short sayings about work, saving and money.
For the last almanack, in 1758, Franklin gathered the best sayings into one long speech. People later printed this speech alone, and it became known as The Way to Wealth.
In the story, Poor Richard stops his horse at a sale of goods, called a vendue. A large crowd is waiting for the sale to begin, and they are talking about hard times.
A man in the crowd turns to Father Abraham, a plain old man with white hair. He asks whether the heavy taxes will ruin the country, and what people should do about them.
Father Abraham stands up slowly and the crowd gathers around him. He promises to be brief, and he says that he will repeat what Poor Richard has written.
Father Abraham agrees that the government taxes are heavy. But he says that people pay far more in other taxes, such as idleness, pride and folly.
Father Abraham reminds the crowd that God helps those who help themselves. Instead of complaining about taxes, he says, we should work to improve our own lives.
Laziness, says Father Abraham, wears us out faster than work does. He compares it to rust, and he says that a key which is often used stays bright.
Father Abraham says that time is the stuff that life is made of. If we waste it, he warns, we waste our lives, because lost time is never found again.
Father Abraham warns against sleeping too much, since sleep takes up so much of our time. There will be plenty of sleeping in the grave, he says, so rise early and work.
Diligence, says Father Abraham, is the mother of good luck. Those who work steadily and carefully usually find that fortune comes to meet them.
Poor Richard's advice is to plough deep while lazy people sleep. Then you will have corn to sell and corn to keep.
One today is worth two tomorrows, says the old man. If you have something to do tomorrow, he advises, do it today.
A person who lives only on hope, says Father Abraham, will go hungry. There are no gains without pains, he says, which means that nothing worth having comes without effort.
A person who has a trade, says Father Abraham, has something like an estate. Hunger may look in at a working man's house, but it will not dare to come inside.
Father Abraham says that if you want your business done well, you should go and do it yourself. The eye of the master, he says, does more work than both his hands.
Want of care, says Father Abraham, does us more harm than want of knowledge. If you never check your workers, he adds, it is like leaving your purse open.
A little neglect may cause a great deal of trouble, says Father Abraham. For want of a nail a shoe was lost, then a horse was lost, and finally the rider was lost.
Hard work is good, Father Abraham says, but a person must also learn to save. Even the gold of the Indies did not make Spain rich, because she spent more than she got.
Many fortunes are spent in the getting of them, says the old man. A person who earns a lot but saves nothing will soon be as poor as before.
A fat kitchen, says Poor Richard, makes a lean will. This means that those who spend too much on food and feasts leave very little behind them.
You may think that a little tea or a little punch can do no harm, says Father Abraham. But many a little makes a great deal, and small costs soon add up to large ones.
Beware of little expenses, says Father Abraham, because a small leak will sink a great ship. A tiny cost may look harmless, but it can wreck a whole fortune over time.
Fools make feasts, says the old man, and wise men eat them. Silks, satins and velvets, he warns, can put out the fire in the kitchen.
Father Abraham points to the goods at the sale and gives a warning. If you buy what you do not need, he says, you may soon have to sell what you do need.
Many people have been ruined by buying cheap goods, says Father Abraham. A bargain is no bargain, he says, if you do not need the thing, and you may only buy regret.
Pride, says Poor Richard, is as loud a beggar as want, and a great deal more rude. A person who wants to look rich will always find that it costs a lot of money.
Pride, says Father Abraham, breakfasted with plenty, dined with poverty and supped with shame. In other words, a proud person who spends too much can lose everything in a short time.
Large ships may go far out to sea, says Poor Richard, but little boats should keep near the shore. In the same way, people should live within their means.
It is easier to resist the first wish, says Father Abraham, than to satisfy all the wishes that follow it. One new luxury, he says, soon leads to another.
Think what you do when you run into debt, says Father Abraham. You give another person power over your freedom, and he may take it whenever he wishes.
The second vice is lying, says Poor Richard, and the first is running into debt. Lying rides upon the back of debt, because a person who owes money soon begins to make false excuses.
Creditors, says Father Abraham, have better memories than debtors. A person who lends money watches every set day very carefully, and the day always seems to arrive too soon.
It is better to go to bed without supper, says Poor Richard, than to wake up in debt. A hungry night is soon forgotten, but a debt can trouble a person for years.
Those who owe money that is to be paid at Easter, says Father Abraham, have a short Lent. Lent is the long period of fasting before Easter, so he means that the time passes quickly.
Experience keeps a dear school, says Poor Richard, but fools will learn in no other. This means that learning from our own mistakes is a very costly way to learn.
An old saying tells us that wise people learn from the mistakes of others. It costs much less to watch someone else fall than to fall yourself.
Content makes poor men rich, says Father Abraham, and discontent makes rich men poor. A person who is satisfied with enough will never feel poor.
Wealth is not his who has it, says Father Abraham, but his who enjoys it. A person who hoards money and never uses it is no richer than a poor man.
For age and want, save while you may, says Poor Richard, because no morning sun lasts a whole day. A person should save when times are good, since good times do not last for ever.
Gain may be uncertain, says Father Abraham, but expense is always certain. It is easier to build two chimneys, he says, than to keep one of them in fuel.
Get what you can, and what you get hold, says Poor Richard. He compares this rule to the magic stone that old scientists believed would turn lead into gold.
Father Abraham says that hard work and careful saving are good, but they are not enough alone. We should also be humble, he adds, because success depends on more than our own efforts.
He that will not be counselled cannot be helped, says Father Abraham. If you will not listen to Reason, he warns, she will surely rap your knuckles.
When his long speech was over, Father Abraham said farewell. He ended with a wise reminder that we can give a person advice, but we cannot give them good conduct.
The people heard the speech and agreed with every word. Then the sale began, and they immediately started to buy goods that they could not afford, as if it had been an ordinary sermon.
Poor Richard realised that the old man had studied his almanacks with great care. He had remembered the sayings from twenty-five years of the book.
Poor Richard had planned to buy cloth for a new coat. After hearing the speech, he went home and decided to wear his old coat a little longer.
More than two hundred years later, the message of The Way to Wealth is still simple. Work hard, spend carefully, stay out of debt, and keep a little for the days ahead.
C1C2: Benjamin Franklin, who was born in Boston in 1706, grew up to become a printer in Philadelphia, a writer, a scientist and one of the founders of his country. Among his many projects was a small yearly book called Poor Richard's Almanack, which he wrote in the voice of an invented and rather poor character named Richard Saunders. People bought it by the thousand, and its sayings were repeated in homes and shops across the colonies.

An almanack in those days was a yearly book that held a calendar, guesses about the weather and a few useful facts for farmers and families. Poor Richard added something more, which was a stream of short and clever sayings about work, thrift and the proper use of money. Some of the sayings were older proverbs that Franklin reworded, and many were his own.

In 1758, for the last year of his almanack, Franklin did something clever: he gathered the best of the sayings into a single speech and wrapped it in a little story. Printed on its own in later years, the piece was given the title The Way to Wealth, and it was translated into many languages. Few pages of advice have ever travelled so far, or been quoted by so many different people.

In the story, Richard Saunders reins in his horse beside a vendue, which is a public sale of merchants' goods, where a great crowd is waiting for the auction to begin. The people are standing about in groups, and, as people do while they wait, they are grumbling about the times and how hard it is to make a living. Their talk, he says, caught his ear, and he decided to stay for a while and to listen to every word.

One of the crowd turned to an old man named Father Abraham, a plain and white-haired figure who was known for his good sense. He asked whether the heavy taxes of the time would not ruin the whole country, and he begged the old man to say what the people ought to do. The crowd fell silent at once, curious to hear what the old man would say about such a weighty question.

Father Abraham rose to his feet, and the crowd drew closer, for they were anxious to hear the opinion of a man who had seen so much of life. He promised to be brief, since a few words are enough for those who are wise, and he warned them that most of what he would say had been said before by Poor Richard. In this way the old man began to speak, and the sayings of the almanack began to flow.

Father Abraham admitted that the taxes were heavy, but he said that we pay other taxes which are a great deal heavier and which no government has ever laid upon us. By our idleness we are taxed twice as much, he said, by our pride three times as much, and by our folly four times as much. These taxes, he added, cannot be lifted by any tax collector, and only we ourselves can reduce them.

There is no use in grumbling, said the old man, for God helps those who help themselves, and we have more power over our fortunes than we like to admit. The person who spends his breath on complaints could spend it on work and, in the end, be a good deal better off. Poor Richard, he reminded them, had said it long before in a few clear words, and he had said it well.

Idleness, the old man declared, is like rust, which eats away a thing faster than ordinary use can wear it down. A key that is used every day stays bright and clean, while the same key left in a drawer turns dull and useless. In the same way, he said, the person who keeps busy is the person who stays sharp.

If you love life, the old man said in words borrowed from Poor Richard, you must not waste time, for time is the very stuff that life is made of. An hour that has gone can never be purchased again with any sum of money, and lost time, as the saying goes, is never found again. The truly prosperous person, in his view, is the one who understands precisely how precious each passing hour is.

Do not sleep away your hours, the old man warned, for there will be sleeping enough in the grave. Poor Richard's rule was early to bed and early to rise, which was said to make a man healthy, wealthy and wise. Modern doctors, it should be said, would add that enough sleep is itself essential to good health.

Diligence is the mother of good luck, the old man announced, and he reminded the crowd that God gives all things to those who work with care. Many people complain about their bad fortune who have never really tried to improve it. Luck, on this view, is largely the reward of steady effort, and it rarely visits the idle.

Plough deep while sluggards sleep, ran the rhyme, and you shall have corn to sell and to keep. The farmer who does his hardest work early in the season enjoys a good harvest, while the idle neighbour has only excuses. Father Abraham could point to many such cases, as every person in the crowd well knew.

Father Abraham pressed the point that one today is worth two tomorrows, for tomorrow may bring new problems, new duties and perhaps no opportunity at all. A task put off is often a task that grows, and the person who says later has already lost half of the work. If there is any duty waiting for tomorrow, he said, then it should be performed today, without delay or excuse.

He that lives upon hope will die fasting, the old man warned, and he added that there are no gains without pains. To wish for a thing is easy, but to earn it requires time, effort and some discomfort, and no amount of dreaming can replace them. This, he said, is the oldest and plainest lesson in the whole business of work, and no one has ever escaped it.

He that has a trade has an estate, the old man said, because a skill is a form of property that cannot easily be taken away by bad luck. At the house of the working man, hunger looks in, but it dares not enter. Here was a comforting thought for the poor, and an instruction for the lazy.

If you want your business done well, the old man said, go and do it yourself, for a servant will rarely care as much as the owner. The eye of the master does more work than both his hands, and the shop that is watched with a careful eye is a shop that makes a profit. This was one of Poor Richard's favourite lessons, and it appears again and again in the almanack.

Want of care does us more damage than want of knowledge, said the old man, for a person who knows the right way and neglects it is worse off than one who has never learned it. To leave one's workers unwatched, he added, is to leave one's purse open for anyone to take. The farmer who hopes to thrive by the plough must either hold it or drive it himself.

A little neglect may breed great mischief, the old man declared, and he quoted an old rhyme about a horse that lost a single nail. For want of the nail the shoe was lost, for want of the shoe the horse was lost, and for want of the horse the rider was lost, and all of it because of one small piece of iron. Small things, he said, should never be despised, for large troubles grow from them.

Industry is excellent, the old man said, but if a person wishes to be wealthy he must think of saving as well as of getting. The gold and silver that flowed to Spain from the Indies, he pointed out, did not make that country rich, because her spending was greater than her income. A river of money will run dry quickly when it runs out as fast as it runs in.

Many a fortune is spent in the very act of getting it, the old man observed, and a person who earns a great deal but saves nothing remains poor in everything but his income. He urged the crowd to learn both skills, for the man who can only get will never keep, and the man who can only keep will never have much to hold. Wealth, he said, stands on both of these legs, and it falls over very quickly if either one is missing.

A fat kitchen makes a lean will, the old man quoted, meaning that the family which spends all its wealth on rich food and fine feasting will have little left to hand down. Everyday comforts are no sin, but they have a way of growing, he said, until they swallow the fortune that paid for them. A small appetite, like a small expense, is the friend of a large estate.

You may think that a little tea, a little punch and a little entertainment now and then can be no great matter, the old man said, but he begged them to remember that many a little makes a mickle. Each small pleasure, taken alone, seems trifling, yet the sum of them over a year is a great sum indeed. It is the quiet and regular spending, rather than the one big purchase, that most often empties a purse.

Beware of little expenses, said Father Abraham, for a small leak will sink a great ship. The captain who ignores a tiny crack in the planks may well find himself at the bottom of the sea, and the man who ignores a daily waste may find himself at the bottom of his purse. A careful watch over small costs, he suggested, is the best protection that a person can have for large ones.

Fools make feasts, and wise men eat them, the old man laughed, and he went on to warn about the cost of fine clothes. Silks and satins, scarlet and velvet, he said, put out the kitchen fire, since the money spent on show is money that cannot be spent on bread and fuel. The crowd laughed too, though some of them looked down at their own clothes.

The old man pointed to the goods that lay ready for the auction and warned the crowd of the danger of such places. Buy what you have no need of, he said, and before long you will sell your necessities, for a bargain is no bargain if it was never needed. His listeners shifted uneasily, aware that the sale was about to begin and that many of them were tempted.

Many have been ruined, the old man said, by buying good bargains, for a low price tempts a person to buy what he does not need and cannot afford. It is foolish, he went on, to lay out good money in a purchase of repentance, which is only another name for regret. Before buying anything at all, then, one should ask whether it is truly needed and whether it can be afforded.

Pride is as loud a beggar as want, the old man said, and a great deal more saucy, for hunger asks for bread while vanity asks for everything. A man who wishes to appear richer than he is must spend more than he has, and the show becomes a heavy chain around his neck. Those who dress above their means, he warned, will soon be bowing to their creditors.

Pride breakfasted with plenty, dined with poverty and supped with infamy, the old man said, drawing a picture of a single day in the life of a proud spender. He starts the morning with a full purse, gets through his fortune by noon, and by evening is reduced to hiding from those to whom he owes money. It was a very short story, but every listener in the crowd could recognise it as his own, or his neighbour's.

Vessels large may venture more, the old man quoted, but little boats should keep near shore, and he meant that a person with a small income should not behave as though he had a large one. To live within one's means is to sail where the water is safe, and to be able to turn for home when the weather changes. The grander the ship, the more it can carry; the smaller the boat, the closer it should stay to land.

It is easier to suppress the first desire, said the old man, than to satisfy all those that follow it, for one luxury makes the next one seem necessary. The family that buys a fine chair soon needs a fine table, and then a fine room to put them in. Like a stone rolling downhill, spending gathers speed as it goes, and it is hard to stop once it begins.

Think what you do when you run in debt, the old man urged, for you give to another person power over your liberty. If you cannot pay at the time that was promised, you will be ashamed to look the lender in the face, and you will become a person who makes excuses and hides. Debt, in short, is a chain, though it may be made of paper rather than iron.

The second vice is lying, the first is running in debt, said the old man, for lying rides upon debt's back, and the person who cannot pay is tempted to deceive. It is hard for an empty bag to stand upright, he added, and a purse that has nothing in it makes a person bend and bow. Honesty is never so difficult as when we owe money that we do not have.

Creditors have better memories than debtors, the old man said, and he described them as a faithful sect who observe fixed days and set times with the greatest care. The debtor may forget the date, but the person he owes will not, and the day of payment arrives sooner than he expected. This remark drew a few uneasy smiles from those who knew it to be true.

Rather go to bed supperless than rise in debt, the old man said, and the crowd smiled at the stern good sense of the saying. A missed supper is forgotten by morning, but a debt follows a person from day to day and from year to year, and it grows heavier with each of them. The man who goes to sleep owing nothing sleeps well, whatever he has had for dinner.

Those have a short Lent, said the old man, who owe money to be paid at Easter, for the days of Lent seem long to those who fast and short to those who dread the bill. The remark would have been clear to his listeners, because Lent was the forty days before Easter that the Christians of the time observed with fasting and prayer. Time runs faster, he meant, when it is carrying us toward a debt, and it never slows down to give us a rest.

Experience keeps a dear school, the old man said, and fools will learn in no other, meaning that the teacher called experience charges a high price for every lesson. A wise person pays the price once and remembers, while a foolish one pays it again and again without improving. He urged his listeners to be pupils of the first kind, and to graduate from that school as soon as they could.

It is wiser to learn from the mistakes of others than to pay for one's own, the old man said, since the first lesson is free and the second is dear. Every ruined merchant and every empty purse in the neighbourhood, he pointed out, was a lesson that cost the listeners nothing. All that was needed was the sense to look at it and to take warning.

Content makes poor men rich, the old man said, and discontent makes rich men poor, for the person who wants everything will never feel that he has enough. Wealth is a feeling as well as a sum, and it is possible to have a great deal of money and still to live in constant want. The wisest course, he suggested, is to learn what is enough and to be glad of it.

Wealth is not his that has it, the old man said, but his that enjoys it, and he reminded the crowd that saving is not the same as hoarding. Money is a servant and not a master, and its purpose is to give a person security, comfort and a little pleasure in the right proportion. A life spent merely in piling up coins has missed the point of them.

For age and want save while you may, the old man said, because no morning sun lasts a whole day. The strong young worker of today will be an old man tomorrow, and the full harvest of this year may be followed by a poor one. A person who saves in the sunshine will have a roof to stand under when the rain arrives.

Gain may be temporary and uncertain, the old man observed, but ever, while we live, expense is constant and certain, and it is easier to build two chimneys than to keep one in fuel. The cost of building a thing is paid once, but the cost of using it goes on every winter and every day. Before taking on a new expense, he advised, a careful person should work out what it will cost in the long run.

Get what you can, and what you get hold, said the old man, for that is the stone that will turn all your lead into gold. He was thinking of the philosopher's stone, which the alchemists of old had searched for in vain, and he told the crowd that the real secret was far cheaper and more reliable. It was thrift and steady work, practised day after day without fail, and they cost nothing to begin.

Industry and frugality are excellent things, the old man concluded, but they may be blasted without the blessing of Heaven, and so we should be humble and not depend upon them alone. He urged his listeners to be generous toward those who were in need and to remember that Job, in the old story, suffered greatly and was afterwards prosperous. The point was that no human plan is entirely safe, and that pride in our own cleverness is a poor foundation.

He that will not be counselled cannot be helped, said the old man, and he added with a smile that if we will not listen to Reason she will surely rap our knuckles. The advice of a friend costs nothing, but the lessons of folly are charged for in full and in advance. He asked only that his hearers turn the sayings over in their minds before they went home.

At last the old man had said all that he wished to say, and he took his leave with a simple farewell. His final words were a modest reminder that anyone may give advice but no one can give good conduct, for the hearer must supply that for himself. The crowd stood quiet for a moment, as people do who have heard something true.

The people heard the speech and approved it, and they immediately did the opposite, just as though it had been a common sermon. For the sale opened at that very moment, and they began to buy extravagantly, in spite of everything they had just been told. It is one of the gentlest and funniest endings in the literature of advice.

Richard Saunders, listening from the edge of the crowd, realised that the good man had studied his almanacks thoroughly and had remembered everything that Poor Richard had dropped on these subjects over twenty-five years. It was a flattering discovery for an author, and he admits that it pleased him. Few writers, after all, hear their own words repeated by a stranger as wise sayings.

Richard was proud to hear his own sayings praised, but he resolved to be the better for the echo of them. He had meant at first to buy cloth for a new coat that very day, and instead he went home determined to wear his old one a little longer. The author, in other words, was the one listener who really took his own advice.

Few pieces of advice have been printed so often or in so many languages as this speech, which has been read in many countries for more than two hundred years. Its message is plain: work steadily, spend with care, stay out of debt and save a little for the days when work is hard. Whether or not a reader ever grows rich, he will be wise to remember Poor Richard's old lesson that small savings are the first step toward freedom.
